utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. This is case number IT-95-5/18-PT, the Prosecutor versus Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Mr. Karadzic, you again appear on your own behalf. Can you just confirm to me at the outset that you can hear interpretation into your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Lordship.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I would take appearances from the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning. Alan Tieger, Hildegard Uertz-Retzlaff, and case manager Iain Reid for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. And I turn my attention to you straight away, Mr. Tieger. As a result of decision of the Appeals Chamber issued at the end of last week, it seems to me inappropriate now for you to seek any further action on your proposed fourth amended indictment in view of the success of your appeal. What action do you propose in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We agree, Your Honour. Thank you. We would move to withdraw the proposed fourth amended indictment. We can do so orally. We can follow up with a written submission, if the Court would prefer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, your oral application here is sufficient for that purpose, and I note the withdrawal, therefore, of the proposed fourth amended indictment. The principal business for this Status Conference is reviewing certain aspects of certain motions which are currently before the Chamber. The first of these is a motion at the instance of the Prosecution requesting the Chamber to invite Lord Owen to testify as a Chamber witness. You Mr. Tieger -- or Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, the accused, Dr. Karadzic, has responded to that motion. Is there anything else to be said on the matter before the Trial Chamber deals with it?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In relation to the motion response, I can actually only say that Rule 85 provides for the Trial Chamber to change the order of the presentation of evidence in the interests of justice, and Rule 98 allows the Trial Chamber to call witnesses. That's all I would like to add. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And in the event that he is a witness in the case, when would you propose that his evidence should be presented? At what stage?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: At the very end, actually. Our planning is that he will be heard in a -- as one of the last witnesses. I mean, after -- at the end of the Prosecution case he would be called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I suppose one incidental benefit of his being a Chamber witness is that you would be entitled to cross-examine him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the reason why we asked for -- for this way of procedure is actually Mr. -- sorry, Lord Owen's wish, and that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's now his wish, but in the Milosevic -- in the Milosevic case, it was the suggestion of the Prosecution, I think. That's what triggered this.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yeah, but it was, at the same time, also a request of Lord Owen, and that's why we actually put it forward, and it went actually well for both sides, I would say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, is there anything you want to add to what you've said so far?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect to Lord Owen with whom I cooperated for a long time, the issue in hand is the way in which the Prosecution will cross-examine, and that is going to be determined whether he is going to be summoned as a Chamber witness or a Prosecution witness. It's not a matter of principle. It's a practical issue, and I stick by my response to the motion. I think that he should not be awarded any special status, because in such a case a cross-examination by the Prosecution would not serve the purposes of the Defence, would be to the benefit of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's assume for the sake of argument that the Prosecution were not to call him and the Trial Chamber were to decide not to invite him as a Chamber witness. What would your position be then? Would you be calling him?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's highly possible that the Defence would seek to summon him. He was main actors in coming the crisis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, thank you to both parties for these further submissions. The Trial Chamber will have to make a decision on this, and that decision will be made fairly soon. The second motion I want to deal with, Dr. Karadzic, is the motion for request for cooperation by the United Nations in support of your efforts to obtain material that's relevant to your Holbrooke Agreement motion. As you know, there was a 65 ter meeting, a meeting under Rule 65 ter, at which I secured your agreement to speak directly to the director of legal affairs of the United Nations, and following that I did so. And following that, as you know, there was an exchange of communication between her office and one your associates, and understand that that matter is now in hand. It seems to me there's nothing more that the Chamber can do in terms of this motion. That doesn't mean to say you can't invoke our assistance in other circumstances, of course you can, but I suggest to you that this particular motion has served its purpose and the appropriate course would be for you to withdraw it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Lordship, I received a response from the UN. Communication has been established, and we've is accepted the conditions offered therein. Now we're only waiting for notification of a date when my legal advisor can visit the New York and Geneva and to collect evidence. We can respond immediately. As soon as they notify us, we will be there. I believe that things are going well, and I believe that important results will ensue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That does not really address the point I'm making to you, which is that the motion appears to have served its purpose and that the appropriate course is for you to withdraw it. And if you don't, then there doesn't seem to be any alternative but for the Trial Chamber to deny the motion as unnecessary now. I was just hoping to avoid unnecessary paperwork.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood you correctly, you mean the motion where I request communication with UN to be established. Is that right? Yes, we can withdraw it since it has served its purpose. Your intervention most probably has helped it to serve its purpose, so thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. I note, therefore, the withdrawal of that motion. The next matter's a lot more complicated, and that is the motion for an order relating to protected Prosecution witnesses. This, again, was the subject of discussion at the 65 ter meeting, and at the end of that meeting, it was left in the hands of the Prosecution to consider how the issues surrounding the volume and the number of witnesses in respect of whom there are protective measures might be dealt with to ensure that this trial is as public as possible. Now, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, can you update me on any developments since that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. What -- what we did during the period, we have actually reviewed the witness situation, and we have, in fact, 159 witnesses that have some form of protective measures. Of those we have contacted 119, and meanwhile we have three witnesses who have expressed willingness that their protective measures be rescinded or changed; and we will file a motion to this effect shortly. However, 88 of these witnesses have specifically asked that their protective measures be continued, and we think they have a valid reason for that. Of those we have not contacted yet, that's -- we -- rather, of those who have not been spoken to about the protective measures within that 119, 23 have protective measures in ongoing cases; and, therefore, we did not address this issue with them, particularly, because we don't see a valid reason to ask them to reconsider it when they have these protective measures ongoing in other cases. However, we have eight witnesses among these 119 for which we did not address this question, particularly, and we will call these witnesses again and speak about protective measures and the need for that. In relation to the 40 witnesses that we have not contacted yet, 13 of those enjoy protective measures in ongoing cases, and we really don't see a reason to call these people. However, the remaining 27, among those are also witnesses whose protective measures date from long time ago, and we will call these witness -- witnesses as a priority to find out whether their situation has changed and whether they would be willing to appear without protective measures or different protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The one category there I don't think I followed was the eight that you referred to.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. These were witnesses -- these eight witnesses have been contacted, but when we were talking to them, we did not address, specifically, the need for protective measures, and we will do that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So does that mean that there are 48 in total who have not been asked the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's correct. No, not exactly. I mentioned also the 23, the 23 among the 119, which have in -- in parallel cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, but for -- otherwise, the figure was correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Our own calculation of the number of witnesses for whom there are protective measures is a bit higher than yours. It's 182, which illustrates just how complex this whole area is, and I will come shortly to a suggestion on how to deal with its complexity, which is one thing, but there's a separate issue from complexity; and that is determining whether the measures should continue, because Dr. Karadzic has raised the point, as a general one, about reviewing the situation where, first of all, there are so many, and secondly, the events that they're speaking about are many years ago now. So one of the things that I raised with you before and which continues to concern me a little is how he can be put in a position of judging -- of trying to judge whether it's appropriate for any request to be made to alter the protective measures; or do you think that that's just something that is not really feasible and on which the assessment of the Prosecution and the information that they have been able to gather is all that will be available?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is always also the Victims and Witnesses Unit who can take a position. What we just find is when the protective measures were granted in the first place, there was a certain reason for this, and if the conditions haven't changed, and, for instance, if victim witnesses are still living in the municipalities where they were victimised and when perpetrators are still at large, I can't really see how they could now be told now, Although the circumstances are the same, you shouldn't have protective measures. And when it comes to other witnesses like, in particular, insider witnesses who may incriminate, in particular, Dr. Karadzic, I can't really -- I think they even -- when they live in areas where they are easily accessible for followers of Dr. Karadzic, I can't really see how they can be now told there 's no need for this any longer. So I think we really have to see whether the circumstances the witnesses find themselves in have changed from what it was before, and if so, then it is a matter of reconsidering; but if it is the same, I just don't see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It may be argued that they have inevitably changed because of the passage of time alone. And if you bear in mind domestic circumstances, the vast majority of witnesses involved in the most serious of criminal cases and domestic circumstances are known to the accused or associates of the accused. It's much less frequent that there are protective measures for witnesses that are capable of concealing their identity from accused people and their associates, because everyone's living in the one community so often in these cases. So there may be, there may be, that's all I say, circumstances in which this institution may be seen as -- as going too far when these measures continue automatically many years after the events themselves and have such a -- or have the capacity to have a major impact on the public nature of the trial. So I'm really looking for guidance on how the accused can be put in a position of making a reasonable assessment of which witnesses he might responsibly make an application to vary the protective measures in relation to. Now, is there anything more you can give me to assist on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, sitting here, one thing occurred to me in terms of the issues the Court raised. It is not a direct response necessarily to the question of the accused's participation or direct participation in the evaluation of the factors, but in comparing the circumstances faced by the Tribunal with domestic circumstances, I would note the differing meaning of "public" in that context. I, for example, come from a jurisdiction, at least in the federal courts, where the broadcasting, televised broadcasting of proceedings is an anathema for a variety of reasons, including the risk to witnesses. So the public nature of the trial is maintained, but it's not amplified in the manner it is in the Tribunal. The Court mentioned that in domestic jurisdictions, the identity of witnesses are, in fact, known to the accused and his associates, by which I assume you mean legal associates and that's the case here as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I didn't mean legal associates. I meant those that might have a criminal connections with an accused in a domestic situation. In other words, a circle that might be able to do something in a situation where the accused, himself, is in custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't consider that to be a positive aspect of the domestic jurisdictions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, but it's a facts of life is all I was suggesting to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I do understand. I'm just suggesting that where that fact of life need not be exacerbated, for example, through televised broadcasting in many jurisdictions that is not done for that reason. Here we do that. That adds another factor that, I think, plays a role in our assessment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it's a very valid comment to point to broadcasting. Just on one other matter that you raised, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, you mentioned that the -- the one positive suggestion you made was that the Victims and Witnesses Section might assist, but in your response to this motion, you've set your face against that as a method of dealing with it. You've indicated they have a part to play but at an appropriate stage, which is after an application has been made and at a late stage in the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, but one can all rely -- as you were looking for ways how to deal with the issue, I was just thinking about -- that maybe a possibility to involve them in that early stage. In particular, they have quite an overview of witnesses from various areas in the -- in the former Yugoslavia, and they may have valid points to make in overall assessment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic, this motion is yours. Is there anything further you wish to say in relation to that motion?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Lordship, I hope that you won't allow the Prosecution to convert this Chamber into a camera obscura. I absolutely oppose that somebody who is not a victim be protected 15, 17, or 20 years after the event. There's no reason for that. And in the erstwhile practice, it has not transpired that any witnesses experienced any inconvenience. Everything is known, and there is no justification for them to be protected. I do not seek any delicate victim to be stripped of their protective measures, but the witnesses, well, can you imagine 200 witnesses using protective measures?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in relation to the more complex aspect of this, which we discussed at the beginning; that is identifying which witnesses, precisely, protective measures apply to and what exactly these measures are in each case. The Chamber has in mind to produce a table of its understanding of the existing protective measures. We are concerned that there have been errors in submissions made to us, and in the latest one, which we received recently - that's the Prosecution notification, the fourth notification of protective measures - there are also errors. Now, that simply underlines just how difficult this whole exercise is. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I'm also concerned when you said, in the beginning on that topic, that you have actually estimated and checked it was more than 180. I was surprised, because we have double-checked it, because of these various figures that we had discussed in the 65 ter Conference, and our -- our finding is it's 159. So there must be some error somewhere or some different views. So it would be definitely very helpful to have a table. We do have a table as well, so we could then basically double-check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is proposed is that a table is compiled showing the Chamber's understanding of the situation, and time is allowed to the parties to make submissions in relation to that with a view to agreement being reached that we have a definitive list of the measures that exist. Now, to make this a worthwhile exercise, we need to know that you've exhausted your intimations to us of the existing measures. Have you done so?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: To my knowledge, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it's -- we've reached the stage where it would be appropriate for us to -- to issue that, I think, for the comments of parties and a final determination of the situation. Apart from anything else, I think it's in everybody's interest be able to refer to one definitive document, which tells us the measures that exist at this stage; and in the absence of any variation between now and the time the witnesses give evidence will apply to the evidence of these witnesses. Mr. Karadzic, that table will give you a complete picture of what exists in the way of protective measures. It may be difficult for you, I understand, to make any detailed comments about the measures and about the table and to assist in correcting it because you're not really in a position to -- to improve on the information available to the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution. The overall picture will assist the Chamber to make a final decision on your motion, but your motion, when it was submitted, related to, I think, 68 witnesses. We now have far more. So what might emerge from all of this for you is a starting point if you wish to apply to the Chamber for variation of the measures which exist. Your point at the moment is a very broad one, that there's no reason to provide protective measures for witnesses who are not victims and that there are obvious categories of victims for whom protective measures exist and should continue, very broad proposition; but you might also want to look at in more detail at the list and the table to see whether, in fact, you feel it appropriate to make more detailed submissions about alterations that might be made to these protective measures. Now, I intend to move on to another subject. On this one is there anything else you wish to say?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you. I shall wait for the opportunity once I have a better insight into the whole situation regarding protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps I can also add one point. We have looked at the categories and type of witnesses, and we have actually 91 victim witnesses with protective measures. That may be of assistance. We have 40 insiders with protective measures, 9 Rule 70 witnesses, and 19 others, like, for instance, intercept operators and the like where the protective measures are -- basically also come from their institutions and where they work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. That's helpful. The next matter I want to deal with is really a formality. The Prosecution have made a motion for reconsideration of the Trial Chamber decision dealing with contact by the Defence with Prosecution witnesses. Now, Dr. Karadzic, this is holding up whatever contact with Defence -- with the Prosecution witnesses is ultimately allowed, and, therefore, it would, I think, be of assistance to your own position if you were able to respond to this fairly quickly. Are you in a position to respond to that this week? The normal deadline would be the 10th of July, but I think it's in everyone's interest that we try to deal with it more quickly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Lordship, if it is necessary for me to file a written motion, I can do that on Monday, the 6th of July. That is the earliest for me. If an oral explanation does not suffice, it would be careless of the Defence to allow the Prosecution to inform us whether anyone agrees to contacts with the Defence or not. This should either be done by the Registry or in some other way, but if necessary, I can promise to file this response on Monday, the 6th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think we would benefit from a written response, so what I will do is order an expedited response by you on the 6th of July. The next matter, Mr. Karadzic, is the Prosecution motion to extend the time again for disclosure of audio files in B/C/S. I think when this arose before and there was an extension granted, you did not object to that. And the Prosecution seek an extension until the 10th of July because of difficulties in translating these -- or, rather, in transferring them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can update you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We actually were very lucky with the reminder of the tapes. Only a few were causing problems. We could disclose yesterday 136 audio files. The only ones that are outstanding now are 40 to 50, and we think we can do it in this week, but they are -- this includes the corrupted ones. So what we did is we asked for ten days to make sure we don't have to come to you, but we are quite confident that we can actually make it faster, but we can't be absolutely sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any objection to that, Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In view of the fact that I haven't reviewed even those that I have received, I have no objection. So you can give them as much time as they need, because I have so much to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. The time will be extended until the 10th of July. Now, Dr. Karadzic, one of the things you've been doing is -- is obtaining from other cases as much of the confidential material as you can. And in relation to one of them, that's the case against Dragan Obrenovic, the order made by the Chamber is inconsistent with a similar order made by the Chamber in the Popovic case. And the Prosecution have now drawn that to our attention and submitted that there are two categories of material which our order covers, which if we were to be consistent with the Popovic decision, would not be included in our order. And the two categories are -- one is personal to Obrenovic's family, and the other relates to character witnesses in his case. Neither would appear to have any relationship with your case, and if you accept that, then I can order -- or, yes, I think we'll probably have to confirm it in writing with the Trial Chamber, but I can deal with this or at least indicate how it will be dealt with. Do you see any problem with this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Basically, no. I think that the Defence can respond positively. On the other hand, I already have a lot of material that I have permission to have access to. As for the things that are not significant for the case, I have absolutely no objections. Namely, questions such as family, et cetera. These are matters that are not of significance to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, the Trial Chamber will vary the previous decision, but because it was a Trial Chamber decision, it's probably necessary to do it in writing.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That deals with the motions that I have on the agenda. One thing I did omit - and I'm sorry I did, but it may be that we can make some progress on it - was the issue of expert witnesses. It was discussed at the Rule 65 ter meeting, and, subsequently, I did a little more to try to find out exactly what was going on, and there have been exchanges of correspondence between your associates and the Office of Legal Aid in the Tribunal. However, the position is still that only one expert has been approved. There are still exchanges of communications about the forensic science and pathology experts. Now, are you up-to-date on what's going on there, Dr. Karadzic, or is that something that's entirely in the hands of a legal associate at this stage?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My legal associates are working in accordance with my instructions fully, and I have filed the curriculum vitae for several experts. And a particularly sensitive issue is the issue of forensic experts, and I intend to conduct a thorough investigation and expertise in view of the sensitivity and the haziness that prevails over certain details. One of my associates has addressed a letter to the Prosecution, actually this morning, in connection with the forensic experts. I have that letter here with me. It goes into some detail, and I expect then it will be much easier to discuss the issue. So I believe that we are making process in this area, too, but this is an enormous amount of material and to be able to respond as to whether we accept or challenge any of this, my legal associates and experts have a great deal of work ahead of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that, but usually that work at the start of the exercise is time-consuming. It's administrative work necessary to set up the exercise. But once the expert is engaged, then it's over to him, and the legal associate can get on with something else. I'm particularly anxious here not to get bogged down in too much communication about the detail, and I am quite happy to get personally involved in dealing with the Tribunal office which manages this matter and your legal associate with a view to speeding this whole exercise up. Please bear that in mind. I know you feel under pressure with the dead-lines that have been set and the volume of material that must be dealt with within these dead-lines, but your associates may feel free to contact the Trial Chamber through Ms. Davidson in front of me if it is felt that direct intervention will assist in cutting through any red tape that might be involved. So I do not want you to feel that you have to deal with this entirely by exchanging correspondence. There may be quicker ways if there are difficulties which need to be resolved. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, I think the same applies. The document to which Mr. Karadzic was referring is a letter, actually, it's probably an e-mail from yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, and we are already working on this. We have disclosed some of the material, in particular exhumation reports and the like, but most of the materials that is actually referred to in this letter we do not have in house, and we are actually contacting ICMP today what their position is on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's very helpful, and you'll appreciate the urgency of it, because we've tried to programme a scheme of dealing with various issues including this one, and there is a date for a response.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. We are dealing with this expeditiously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, does either party -- well, let me deal with you first of all, Dr. Karadzic. Do you have any other matter in relation to any of the motions that you wish to raise?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that I have nothing in particular at this point in time. However, as you well know, the motion, in connection with the agreement with Holbrooke, is awaiting additional information from the UN. As you know, the American government has challenged this, and we have filed a submission asking for contact with two officials. The Swedish government -- or, rather, the minister, Mr. Bildt, is willing to communicate with the Defence, but just now they're busy with the fact that they have taken over the chairmanship of the European Union, so I believe that this contact will be made by the middle of this month. So this is something that we're working on very expeditiously, and we hope that the Chamber will soon give thought to a procedure whereby it would be possible to establish, once and for all, whether such an agreement existed or not. Then there's a question of the Judge, but I don't think I have anything in particular at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: As you rightly point out, both of these matters are in hand. The Chamber, or at least I have certainly indicated to you that your Holbrooke motion does require to be dealt with it, and the Chamber is actively considering how to deal with that, and you may find that a decision on that is made fairly soon. The other point is out with my control and in the hands of others. Sorry, is there any matter in relation to any motion, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, that you wish to raise?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I want to of move, then, on to a quite separate subject, and that is a very preliminary consideration of the scope that there might be to apply rules within Rule 73 bis in relation to this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: As parties are aware, a Pre-Trial Conference has been set for the 20th of July. It's now clear to the Trial Chamber that that date is not realistic and that this trial will not start as soon as that, but -- and is unlikely to start prior to September. So even the Pre-Trial Conference, I anticipate, will not be before September. So you can score out the plan for the 20th of July. However, that's no reason for not, at least, looking at the issue of -- of how the trial might be made more manageable by application of these rules. And what I'm really seeking is your assistance, that's both parties' assistance, in identifying the areas in which there might be scope for reducing the size of the trial. The matter has arisen before. It's some time ago, I think, since any submission was made about it. Dr. Karadzic made submissions many months ago about this, but they were not followed up in writing, in spite of an indication being given that in dealing with the preliminary motions they might have been. That doesn't necessarily mean that you've departed from thoughts that you had before about how the scope of the trial might be more concentrated. Do you have any initial thoughts on that, Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should, first of all, like to express gratitude for the patience the Chamber has shown in connection with the agreement with Holbrooke, and I hope that no decision will be made until we have provided the information we're expecting and that there will be an occasion for us to have an evidentiary hearing in connection with that agreement. As for September, I don't know whether you had in mind September this year as the date for the beginning of trial, because the material I have requires months and months of time just to look through it, to classify it, to give instructions to Defence teams in the field to do their investigation. So I'd like to know September which year you're planning for the beginning of trial. As for the scope of the indictment, I'm really surprised why the Prosecution has engaged in such a voluminous undertaking. Because from the standpoint of proving the truth and forming a puzzle of the truth, I have no objections, but this is such a vast trial, that it will last for years, and it will require enormous funds. And would I not object at all if the Prosecution were to shorten or eliminate certain things and make the process more effective and more focussed rather than amassing 200 or 300 witnesses under Rule 92 bis, which is making the whole trial more problematic. It would be less so if the Prosecution were to focus on certain fundamental issues if they did have such issues, but I am quite confident that they don't have a case against me. So they're trying to hit me with an air rifle. I don't want to be unpleasant. I think that I would be far more successful if I were to accused them of more minor infringements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm -- the Prosecution is happy to talk with the Court concreting about any aspect of case it sees fit, but since the matter was raised broadly by the accused in terms of making the presentation more effectively, identifying the fundamental issues, and so on, I think it's incumbent upon me to note that, as expressed in the previous Status Conference, I believe, there was some expectation about the impact of the accused's anticipated compliance with Rule 65 ter and the provision of a pre-trial brief which would, indeed, narrow those issues. Notwithstanding the assurances made at that Status Conference and an order by the Court that tracked those assurances, that has not been done. And any objective of Rule 65 ter toward narrowing the issues, and I think that is a large part of 65 ter (G), are not available to us for that reason. More broadly, I'd say in terms of fundamental issues in the case, I don't think it's necessary for the Prosecution to say that the components of the case that we've identified, the alleged ethnic cleansing of 1992 through 1995, the siege of Sarajevo, the events in Srebrenica, are rather fundamental issues, and we certainly intend to pursue those in the most effective and expeditious way. But the suggestion that those can be dispensed with by focusing on something that might be characterised as more fundamental issues I don't think is helpful. I think the provision of a pre-trial brief that comply with Rule 65 ter would have been vastly more -- of vastly more assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The pre-trial brief is only now in my hands. I note your remarks, which I think relate to the lack of concentration on factual issues in it, in any detail at all. And the consequences of that will have to be considered and, if appropriate, then steps will be taken, but that may or may not be possible. I'm not in a position to comment. However, what I understand by more fundamental issues from Mr. Karadzic is a reference to evidence of his individual criminal responsibility, and I think the suggestion from his point of view that it would be helpful to everyone to identify clearly the evidence that points to that. Have you given thought at all to -- to the time that's likely to be necessary to present the Prosecution case?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I guess, I don't want to say of course because I don't know that it was necessarily a rhetorical question, but we certainly considered in a variety of ways as we were producing, for example, the witness list. We continue to look at the time required to present the case. If, and I don't want to re-interpret the Court's questions because I'm sure the Court can do that much more effectively for me, but if the Court is asking us to reconsider, for example, individual time assessments for witnesses, whether or not there are witnesses whose evidence overlaps, and whether or not some more economical approach can be used, I can assure the Court that we certainly do that on an ongoing basis and will continue to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But from my use of, I think, an American expression, do you not have in your preparations a ballpark figure for the time that you expect the case to take, from the Prosecution point of view? In other words, how many hours you think presenting your case will take.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We do, Your Honour, and I think that's -- that's encapsulated in the summary of -- or in the aggregation of the times for the witness presentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what does that come to?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's approximately 490 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that calculation based on the assumption that the various 92 bis, et cetera, motions will be granted?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. It incorporates those figures based on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You appreciate that taking, just for the broad purposes of a very rough calculation, 60 per cent of that time for cross-examination and maybe 10 per cent of the total for all the administration that goes on in the course of the presentation of the evidence, we're talking about a period, I think, significantly in excess of a year for the presentation of the Prosecution case. Is that consistent with your understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I mean sitting five days a week, four hours a day, it would take 43 weeks, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think that would be for the -- for the total case incorporating the cross-examination and the administrative matters, yes, I think that's about right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But being realistic, things never work that way, do they. You don't manage to pack it into 43 weeks, 5 days a week. So it's going to be -- and 43 weeks is probably longer than a year itself when you take interruptions for leave and other reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is a reality, of course, that we face, but it can be narrowed as we've seen in comparison with different court practices.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And, indeed, it can be expanded, depending on the decisions made in relation to your motions. So we may have to be talking -- we may have to be talking about other ways of looking at this. I mean, I understand your point that Srebrenica might be seen as the discrete element, Sarajevo, and the ethic cleansing; but if you take the ethnic cleansing on its own, it's not immediately obvious why there must be 27 municipalities dealt with individually. It may be that the fourth element which you haven't mentioned in the indictment, that of the hostage taking, perhaps is an element that we just don't have the luxury of the necessary time to deal with it. It may be we don't have time to do both Srebrenica and Sarajevo. I don't know. I think this is going to have to be a much more intensive debate, but probably in September. My purpose in putting this on the agenda today was so that we don't leave here unaware of each other's perception of this issue and the need to be creative, I think, in our thinking if we want to ensure that the largest possible volume of material in relation to all these issues can, in fact, be presented in the course of a trial. Now, that exhausts the agenda I have. Dr. Karadzic, is there any other matter that we have not so far discussed that you wish to raise?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Lordship. I would like to revisit the issue of protective measures for one witness - I will not mention that witness's name - from an important (redacted). I seek that protective measures be removed or for him to be removed from the witness list. I would like him to be a witness but without those measures, because that agency, unfortunately, perform activities which are unacceptable in our territory, and I would like to look into this. Another thing I'd like to say is that I was a bit relieved, because I see that the Prosecution does not want us to work in two shifts, eight or ten hours a day, or four- or five-day working week. Maybe we should consider working in three shifts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That may not be their decision. You haven't seen the 24-hour-a-day sitting schedule, have you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, given the volume and the planning involved, maybe it would be a useful precedent, who knows? So far as issues that I'm supposed to raise are concerned, may I remind you that I requested from 24 countries and two international organisations to provide certain information. We are waiting for their replies. Eighteen out of them have not responded, five of them responded to the fact that they are going to consider my motion, and three of them rejected to furnish voluntarily such information, and, unfortunately, I will have to seek redress from the Chamber. Unfortunately, this is the first wave of information that I'm seeking from international organisations and countries. I foresee more problems when I seek to be furnished with sensitive information and data. I believe that all countries supporting the work of this Tribunal have to furnish everything that will help us get to the truth. Of course I observe Rule 70 and their concerns about protection of their confidential information, but they should have no secret before this Trial Chamber. This is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. I note what you say. The matter you raise in relation to protective measures will require a motion in writing. It doesn't need to be too complex, but it does need to reflect the -- some detail of the reasons for seeking that variation. Mr. Tieger, is there any other matter that you wish to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is a courtroom booked at present for the morning of the 22nd of July for a further Status Conference. It's not clear at this stage if that will be necessary. If it is, then a Scheduling Order will be issued at least a week beforehand. Failing that, there will be a Status Conference in the course of August, the details of which would -- will be intimated, but exactly when that one takes place will depend on necessity: What work is there that requires the attention of the Pre-Trial Judge in the course of a Status Conference. Meanwhile, we will continue to deal as expeditiously as possible with the various matters which are currently before us, and we will give it further consideration to the briefs submitted by the Prosecution and by the accused and decide if any further action is required on these. You have something else, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Lordship, I do have, to wit I was supposed to receive by the 16th of June translation into Serbian of the motion concerning adjudicated facts. I have not received it yet, so I'm not sure whether I will be able to stick to the dead-line of the 14th of July, which I could theoretically observe since I have to respond to the second motion concerning adjudicate the facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm concerned to learn of this, and I will make inquiries immediately after this sitting to find out what the position is. I would certainly not expect you to respond by the 14th of July, if you have not yet received it. So in the light of the information I get, I will give you an alternative date for responding, which will allow you at least the same time as you would have had, which is what, four weeks from the time that you have the translated version. So an adjustment will be made to accommodate that. Thank you. So that completes the work of the Status Conference, which is now adjourned.
